lead: Full gradient descent computes the loss gradient over all N training samples before one update. Stochastic gradient descent replaces that full gradient with an estimate from one sample; mini-batch gradient descent uses B samples. Each step is cheap, so many updates fit in the same time. The estimate is noisy, but the noise helps: it shakes training out of flat regions and saddles. This is the default training loop for deep networks, from image classifiers on a phone to language models on a cluster.
prereq: You need: 2.1 for the update rule and the learning rate.

sections.h3: One sample, B samples, or all N

blocks.text: Full-batch gradient descent uses the average gradient over all N samples. Let N be the number of training samples, θ the parameter vector, η the learning rate, and ℓ<sub>i</sub>(θ) the loss on sample i. The full gradient is g = (1/N) Σ<sub>i=1</sub><sup>N</sup> ∇ℓ<sub>i</sub>(θ). One update needs a pass over all N samples. When N is large, that is too expensive.
Mini-batch gradient descent uses a random set B<sub>t</sub> of B sample indices. The update is:

blocks.where: θ<sub>t</sub> is the parameter vector after t updates; η is the learning rate, a positive step size; B<sub>t</sub> is the set of indices in batch t (size B); ∇ℓ<sub>i</sub>(θ<sub>t</sub>) is the gradient of sample i's loss at θ<sub>t</sub>; B is the batch size.

blocks.text: Plain SGD is B = 1; some syllabi call it on-line learning. A mini-batch uses B > 1, commonly 32, 64, 128 or 256. Powers of two map well to GPU and TPU memory. The batch gradient g<sub>B</sub> is an estimate of g. An epoch is one pass over all N samples. An iteration is one update. If N is divisible by B, iterations per epoch = N/B. If not, the last batch is smaller, so use ⌈N/B⌉ iterations.

items: Draw a random permutation of the N sample indices.
Cut it into batches of B; the last batch may be smaller.
For each batch, compute the average sample gradient and apply one update.
After the last batch, the epoch ends.

blocks.text: The figure uses N = 12 and B = 4, so one epoch has three batches.

Draw the batch uniformly at random. Then E[g<sub>B</sub>] = g. The mini-batch gradient is unbiased: its average over all possible batches equals the full gradient. If one sample's gradient has variance σ² and samples are independent, then the batch gradient has variance:

blocks.where: g<sub>B</sub> is the mini-batch gradient; σ<sup>2</sup> is the variance of the single-sample gradient; B is the number of samples in the batch. The standard deviation is σ/√B.

blocks.text: Doubling B halves the variance and divides the standard deviation by √2. The estimate is still noisy, but less noisy. Noise is not only a cost. In a flat region or at a saddle point, the full gradient is near zero and full-batch descent can stall. The random part of g<sub>B</sub> gives a push. Too much noise, however, makes the final steps jump around, so B and η must be chosen together.

Linear scaling heuristic: if you multiply B by k, try multiplying η by k. A batch k times larger has variance k times smaller, so a larger step may keep similar progress. This is a heuristic, not a law; check the loss and validation score. Momentum smooths this noise; see 2.3.

Shuffle the order every epoch. Without shuffling, the network sees the same sample order and often the same class order in every epoch. Batches become correlated, the gradient can oscillate, and the model can fit order rather than content. A fresh random permutation each epoch makes batches different.

Small batches give a cheap update but a high-variance estimate. If B is very small, one unusual sample can dominate the step. Large batches give a reliable gradient but cost more per update and may need a larger η; they also give fewer updates per epoch. Use the largest B that fits memory and still trains well, then tune η.

One epoch is not one update. With N = 1000 and B = 100, one epoch has 10 updates. Comparing SGD steps with gradient descent epochs is a factor-of-ten error here. Record iterations, epochs and updates separately.

items: If loss spikes, lower η or raise B.
If progress is slow, raise η cautiously.

figure.caption: With N = 1000 and B = 100, one epoch gives 10 updates instead of 1, so 20 epochs give 200 updates against 20; averaging 100 samples shrinks the gradient spread from about 0.632 to about 0.063.

examples.question: A UPI fraud classifier has N = 1000 labelled transactions. You train with mini-batch gradient descent using B = 100 for 20 epochs. (a) How many iterations per epoch? (b) How many weight updates? (c) How many updates would full-batch gradient descent make in the same 20 epochs? (d) One sample's gradient has variance 0.4. Find the variance and standard deviation of the mini-batch gradient, assuming independent samples.
steps: Iterations per epoch = N/B = 1000/100 = 10 iterations per epoch.
Weight updates in 20 epochs = epochs × iterations per epoch = 20 × 10 = 200 updates.
Full-batch gradient descent makes one update per epoch, so 20 epochs × 1 = 20 updates.
Mini-batch standard deviation = √0.004 ≈ 0.0632, rounded to 0.063 gradient units.
examples.answer: With B = 100 there are 10 iterations per epoch, 200 weight updates in 20 epochs, 20 full-batch updates, and the mini-batch gradient has variance 0.004 and standard deviation about 0.063 gradient units.
examples.check:
N = 1000
B = 100
epochs = 20
sigma2 = 0.4
iter_per_epoch = N // B
updates = epochs * iter_per_epoch
full_updates = epochs
var_batch = sigma2 / B
std_batch = var_batch ** 0.5
print(iter_per_epoch)
print(updates)
print(full_updates)
print(var_batch)
print(round(std_batch, 3))

traps: Calling an epoch an iteration. An epoch has N/B iterations when batches are full; only full-batch descent has one update per epoch.
Comparing SGD steps with gradient descent epochs. With N = 1000 and B = 100, 20 SGD epochs are 200 updates, not 20.
Forgetting to shuffle. Fixed order makes batches correlated and can teach the model the order of classes rather than the features.
Using a tiny batch and blaming the learning rate. A very small B gives a high-variance gradient estimate; the direction itself is unreliable.
Treating linear scaling as a law. Multiplying B by k and η by k is only a starting guess; large steps can diverge.

quiz.q: Define epoch and iteration in mini-batch gradient descent.
quiz.a: An epoch is one pass over all N training samples. An iteration is one parameter update using one mini-batch.

quiz.q: What is plain SGD in terms of batch size B?
quiz.a: Plain SGD uses B = 1 sample per update; some syllabi call it on-line learning.

quiz.q: Why is the mini-batch gradient called unbiased?
quiz.a: If each batch is drawn uniformly at random, the expected value of the mini-batch gradient over all batches equals the full gradient: E[g<sub>B</sub>] = g.

quiz.q: N = 5000, B = 250, 12 epochs. Find iterations per epoch and total updates.
A single-sample gradient has variance 1.2. For B = 64, find the mini-batch variance and standard deviation.
Why does the linear scaling heuristic suggest raising η when B is raised?
quiz.a: A batch k times larger has variance k times smaller, so the gradient estimate is less noisy. A step k times larger keeps a similar scale of parameter movement. It is a heuristic because curvature, optimizer state and clipping change the safe step.

quiz.q: A training script does not shuffle and compares 20 SGD epochs with 20 full-batch epochs. What two errors can result?
quiz.a: Without shuffling, batches repeat the same order and class order, so gradients are correlated and the model can fit order. Also 20 SGD epochs with N/B = 10 give 200 updates, while 20 full-batch epochs give 20 updates; comparing them as equal updates is wrong.

beyond: Not for the exam. Large-scale training uses data-parallel mini-batches across many accelerators, and the linear scaling rule becomes a starting point rather than a guarantee. Researchers measure the gradient noise scale to decide when a larger batch is worth the extra compute. Search for gradient noise scale, linear scaling rule, large-batch training and learning-rate warmup.
